solutions.check: 31 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: A failure to indulge can, if put in need

indicators.note: To put a thing in something is to lodge it inside, and the if only softens the instruction into the sentence.

parts.note: the absence of a thing is the need for it, and the word parts after its third letter
a tin is the can on the shelf

explanation.surface: Someone giving in to temptation, with a can put by against a rainy day.
explanation.walkthrough: Need reads as the verb the sentence wants and is a noun in the wordplay: a lack, a going-without. Can looks like the modal verb sitting in the middle of the sentence and is the thing on the shelf.
explanation.definitionFit: Abstinence is the deliberate going-without of drink, food or sex when it is on offer, so the clue names it by what does not happen.

clue.text: 'Settled last conflict': Trump's top loyal supporter

indicators.note: Something that has settled has dropped into whatever arrangement it came to rest in, which is not the one it started in.

parts.note: the four letters of the word redealt
a war is armed conflict between states

indicators.note: The top of a name is its head, so the letter wanted is the one it begins with.

parts.note: the letter the name starts with, taken as instructed

explanation.surface: A headline declaring the last war over, quoted from the chief of Trump's followers.
explanation.walkthrough: Settled reads as the end of the fighting and is the instruction that unsettles four letters. The quotation marks are surface dressing: nothing inside them is being said aloud or used as a sound.
explanation.definitionFit: A stalwart is the one who stays with a cause when the rest drift away, which is what makes a supporter loyal rather than merely present.

clue.text: One-time ejaculation, say, before one died

parts.note: e.g. is the Latin exempli gratia, which reads as say or for example
a is the article, and one of a thing is a thing
d is the short form on gravestones and in genealogies

explanation.surface: The sort of cry a person lets out shortly before dying.
explanation.walkthrough: Ejaculation is the old sense, a sudden cry, which is why the definition calls it one-time: nobody has used the word that way in a century. All three pieces are conventions dropped in without any signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Egad is an archaic softened oath for 'by God', an exclamation last in earnest use around the eighteenth century, which is what one-time marks.

clue.text: Pence, sweetheart, is FAKE!

parts.note: p is the coin, the pence on any British price tag
honey is what you call a sweetheart

explanation.surface: Somebody calling Mike Pence a fake, with an endearment thrown in.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital letter makes Pence the vice-president while the wordplay wants the coin. FAKE is shouted in capitals for the surface's benefit and carries no instruction at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Something phoney is passing itself off as what it is not, which is what calling it fake says outright.

clue.text: It's not good to be upstanding

indicators.note: Something upstanding has been set on its end, and a down entry read from the foot upward gives its letters back to front.

parts.note: to be, in the sense of to exist, is to live, and the word is then read upward

explanation.surface: A suggestion that being upright and honest does nobody any favours.
explanation.walkthrough: Upstanding means respectable in the sentence and means standing on its head in the wordplay. To be is the verb to exist, which setters write as LIVE more readily than any dictionary would.
explanation.definitionFit: Evil is wickedness itself rather than mere badness, so 'not good' is about as far as understatement will stretch.

clue.text: Regally unsound, producing an adverse reaction

indicators.note: Something unsound has not been put together properly, and letters not put together properly are not in the order they were given.

parts.note: seven letters of fodder, the word taken whole

explanation.surface: Behaving in a kingly way, shakily, and provoking a bad response.
explanation.walkthrough: Regally looks like an adverb describing how the unsoundness is done and is the raw material. An adverse reaction is meant medically here, not as the frosty response the surface pictures.
explanation.definitionFit: An allergy is the body's hostile response to something harmless — pollen, peanuts, cats — which is an adverse reaction in the clinical sense.

clue.text: Getting leg over sailor love is deliberate damage!

indicators.note: What lies over something covers it, so the word named splits and the next pieces sit in the gap.

parts.note: a leg of a race or a journey is a stage of it, and the word parts after its first letter
an AB is an able seaman, the Navy's rating for an ordinary sailor
love is the tennis scoreboard's nothing, written as a ring

explanation.surface: Going to bed with a sailor, and calling the result damage done on purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: Getting your leg over is British slang for having sex, which is the whole of the sentence; leg is quietly a stage of a race instead. The exclamation mark sells the outrage and instructs nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Sabotage is wrecking something on purpose — a machine, a plan, a negotiation — so deliberate damage names both the intent and the act.

clue.text: Desert Fergie (stuffed by opening bits of horrendous apology)

indicators.note: To be stuffed by something is to have it pushed into you, so the name splits and takes the letters that follow.

parts.note: Fergie is Sarah Ferguson, Duchess of York and ex-wife of Prince Andrew; the clue takes her first name in its four-letter form and parts it after the second letter

indicators.note: The opening bit of a word is where it starts, and the plural says each of the two words gives up its first letter.

parts.note: the letter each word opens with, taken as instructed

explanation.surface: Walking out on the Duchess of York in the middle of a dreadful apology.
explanation.walkthrough: Desert is the verb the sentence needs and the noun the answer is, which is the whole of the misdirection. The brackets park the instructions out of the sentence's way without breaking it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sahara is the great sand desert across northern Africa, so the clue names the kind of place by its largest single instance.

clue.text: House messed up after Sun gets to dig the dirt?

indicators.note: What comes after a thing follows it, so the house is written second even though the clue names it first.

parts.note: s is the short form of sun, as on a weather chart
a hovel is a squalid, broken-down house

explanation.surface: A household wrecked once the Sun has dug up the dirt on it.
explanation.walkthrough: Sun is the tabloid in the sentence and the weather chart's single letter in the wordplay. Messed up looks like an instruction to shuffle and is part of the description instead.
explanation.definitionFit: To shovel is to move earth with a broad blade, so dig the dirt names the work while the question mark nods at the scandal sense.

clue.text: Raffles almost the lot off?

definitions.note: Raffles is one particular establishment rather than a word for such places in general, so the clue defines a class by its most famous member and the question mark is the licence for it.

indicators.note: A phrase given almost in full stops just short of its end, so the final letter never arrives.
Something that has gone off is not as it should be, and letters not as they should be have left their printed order.

parts.note: five letters of fodder: the two words with the final letter docked as instructed

explanation.surface: The gentleman burglar Raffles making off with very nearly everything.
explanation.walkthrough: Raffles is E. W. Hornung's gentleman thief, which is the story the sentence tells; the one the definition means stands on Beach Road in Singapore. Off is the only instruction, and it looks like part of the theft.
explanation.definitionFit: Raffles is the grand colonial hotel in Singapore, home of the Singapore Sling, so the name stands as one instance of the class.

clue.text: Dome's changed name — that's familiar

indicators.note: Something changed is no longer as it was, and letters no longer as they were come out in a new order.

parts.note: the four letters of the word redealt
n is the short form of name, as on a form

explanation.surface: The Dome under yet another new name, which rings a bell.
explanation.walkthrough: Familiar reads as the adjective and is a noun: the spirit that attends a witch, usually in animal shape. The Dome is the Millennium Dome at Greenwich, renamed for its sponsors more than once.
explanation.definitionFit: A familiar is the attendant spirit a witch keeps, and the witch trials took those spirits to be demons wearing an animal's shape.

clue.text: A trauma covered up by the state — "it's cosmetic"

indicators.note: To be covered up by something is to have it laid over you on both sides, so the letters named next close round what has just been written.

parts.note: MA is the two-letter postal code for Massachusetts, and the pair parts to take what it covers
the article, taken as it stands
a scar is the mark an injury leaves, and trauma is the medical word for that injury

explanation.surface: A wound hushed up by the authorities and dismissed as merely skin-deep.
explanation.walkthrough: Cosmetic reads as the adjective — a change that is only for show — and the definition wants the noun. The state is a US one: Massachusetts, whose postal code is the two letters doing the covering.
explanation.definitionFit: Mascara is the cosmetic brushed onto the lashes, so the clue names it by the class of product it sits in on the shelf.

clue.text: (& 30ac.) Leonard seen out to get a Reform UK member

indicators.note: Something out is out of place, and letters out of place are not standing in the order they were printed in.

parts.note: eleven letters of fodder, the two words redealt together

explanation.surface: Leonard being escorted off the premises so that a Reform UK man can be caught.
explanation.walkthrough: Seen out reads as showing a guest to the door and is the shuffle. Lee Anderson is the MP for Ashfield who left the Conservatives for Reform UK in 2024, and the answer runs 3 then 8 across two entries.
explanation.definitionFit: Lee Anderson sits in the Commons for Reform UK, Nigel Farage's party, so the clue names him as one of the handful who do.

clue.text: Harry bolted wine

parts.note: a horse that bolted ran
sack is the old fortified white wine out of Spain, the stuff Falstaff drinks

explanation.surface: Prince Harry making off with the wine.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital makes Harry the prince, and it is a plain verb meaning to raid and lay waste. Sack is Elizabethan for sherry, a word kept alive by Shakespeare and by crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: To harry a place is to raid it and strip it bare, which is what ransacking a house comes to: turned over and emptied.

clue.text: see 24ac.
Bound to take in laundry ultimately for the Cambridge lot?

definitions.note: The Cambridge lot names one particular group of agents rather than any such group, so the clue defines the class by its most famous case and the question mark licenses it.

indicators.note: To take something in is to admit it inside, so the word named parts and the letter goes into the gap.

parts.note: to bound along is to spring, and the word parts after its second letter

indicators.note: What comes ultimately comes at the very end, so the letter wanted is the one the word finishes on.

parts.note: the letter the word ends on, taken as instructed

explanation.surface: Being obliged to collect the laundry for the Cambridge crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: Bound reads as obliged and means leap. The Cambridge lot are Burgess, Maclean, Philby and Blunt, undergraduates recruited by Moscow in the 1930s and the most notorious traitors Britain has produced.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cambridge men worked as a circle of Soviet agents inside the British establishment, which is what a ring of spies is.

clue.text: Half in limbo, I'm affected by Home Counties freeze

indicators.note: Something affected has been acted on and altered, and letters altered do not keep the arrangement they came in.

parts.note: one letter of fodder, half of the two-letter word as instructed

indicators.note: A word given in half hands over only part of itself, and half of a two-letter word is the letter it starts with.

parts.note: five more letters of fodder, the word taken whole
two more, the apostrophe read through
the Home Counties are the ring of English counties around London, all of them in the south-east

explanation.surface: Stuck half in limbo and feeling the cold snap out in the commuter belt.
explanation.walkthrough: In is the smallest fodder a clue can halve, and the half wanted is the one that joins onto what follows. Freeze is the definition and the weather of the sentence at the same time.
explanation.definitionFit: To immobilise something is to stop it moving at all, which is freeze in the sense of an order barked at a person rather than what water does.

clue.text: Farage's thing? It's a nominal nightmare!

definitions.note: The definition names the cause a man is identified with rather than offering a synonym for it, and the question mark is the setter's licence for that.

indicators.note: A nightmare is a thing gone thoroughly wrong, and letters gone thoroughly wrong stand in no order anyone chose.

parts.note: eleven letters of fodder, the apostrophe read through

explanation.surface: Farage's pet subject, written off as a nightmare in name alone.
explanation.walkthrough: Nominal means in name only, which is the verdict the sentence delivers, and its letters are the raw material. Nigel Farage has led UKIP, the Brexit Party and now Reform UK, all on the one cause.
explanation.definitionFit: Nationalism is the my-country-first politics every party Farage has fronted has been built on, so the clue names it as his stock in trade.

clue.text: Immoderate as a blow-up doll?

definitions.note: The second half names a thing the word describes rather than another word for it, so a comparison stands where a synonym would; the question mark marks the stretch.
definitions.meaning: the figurative sense, of prices and claims swollen past reason
the literal sense, of something pumped full of air

explanation.surface: A jibe measuring somebody's excess against a sex toy.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are the same word, and the only joinery is the as that holds the comparison together. Prices and reputations take the figurative sense; the doll takes the foot pump.
explanation.definitionFit: Prices, egos and expenses are called inflated once they have swollen past what is reasonable, which is immoderate, while a blow-up doll is inflated in the plain air-pump sense.

clue.text: Gnome's English with two farm animals

parts.note: e is the standing short form of english
the first of the pair, the one kept for bacon
the second, the uncastrated male sheep

explanation.surface: A garden gnome, English, posed between a couple of farm animals.
explanation.walkthrough: A gnome is a pithy maxim as well as a lawn ornament — the Greek word for a saying, which is where gnomic comes from. The clue never says which farm animals, and only one pair joins up into anything.
explanation.definitionFit: A gnome in its older sense is a short pointed maxim, and an epigram is that same thing: a thought sharpened down to a line or two.

clue.text: TV pundit right to be kicked out of northern city

indicators.note: Whatever is kicked out of a place has gone from it, so the letter named leaves the word it was sitting in.

parts.note: Preston is a city in Lancashire, in the north-west of England, and it is the word being worked on
r is the short form of right, and this is the letter that goes

explanation.surface: A television commentator who thoroughly deserves running out of a northern city.
explanation.walkthrough: Right reads as the judgement — right to be kicked out — and is a single letter. Robert Peston is ITV's political editor, on screen outside Downing Street most weeks of the year.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Peston fronts ITV's political coverage and his own weekly show, which makes him a pundit in the television sense of the word.

clue.text: Cloak from a time before phone messaging?

parts.note: pre- is the prefix for whatever comes earlier, as in pre-war
a text is the message sent from a phone

explanation.surface: A cloak dating from the days before anybody texted.
explanation.walkthrough: Cloak is the noun that hides a motive, not the garment the sentence hangs up. The joke is that the era before texting really would be the pre-text one, hyphen and all.
explanation.definitionFit: A pretext is the false reason offered to cover the real one, so cloak names it by what it does: throwing cover over the truth.

clue.text: Ireland welcomes politician's "not possessed by UK now"

definitions.note: The definition describes the answer by what has been lost rather than naming it, so a whole phrase stands where a noun would, carried as somebody's quoted remark.

indicators.note: To welcome someone is to take them in, so the country's letters part and the next piece steps inside.

parts.note: Eire is the Irish state's own name for itself, and the word parts after its first letter
an MP is a Member of Parliament, the crossword's standing politician

explanation.surface: Ireland taking in a politician who says the UK has lost its grip on things.
explanation.walkthrough: Ireland is the country's own name in the wordplay rather than the English one. The quoted half is where the politics sits: Hong Kong, the last colony of any size, went back to China in 1997.
explanation.definitionFit: The British Empire is the possession the UK once had and has not had for decades, so the clue defines it entirely by its loss.

clue.text: Genial as two fellows and a bishop covered in piss

indicators.note: Whatever is covered in something has it all over the outside, so the drink closes round the letters just named.

parts.note: British slang is happy to call beer piss, and ale is the beer word that fits; it parts after its first letter
f is the short form of fellow, and the clue asks for two of them
the article, taken as it stands
b is the bishop on a chess scoresheet

explanation.surface: A pair of colleagues and a bishop drenched in beer, all very good-humoured about it.
explanation.walkthrough: Two fellows are the letter doubled rather than two men, and fellow and bishop are both single-letter conventions — one out of the academic world, one off the chessboard. Piss is the Eye's word for the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone affable is easy to fall into talk with and pleasant with it, which is what genial describes in a host or a companion.

clue.text: (& 14dn.) Go through marriage ceremony? Piss off!

definitions.meaning: the tying-the-knot sense, read as a plain instruction
the brush-off, yelled at somebody you want rid of

explanation.surface: Somebody asked about getting married and telling the asker exactly where to go.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are the same two words: tying the knot is the wedding, and the same phrase shouted is the send-off. The answer runs 3 then 7 across two entries.
explanation.definitionFit: Tying the knot is marrying, so the phrase covers the ceremony; hurled at someone, the same words are the British way of telling them to clear off.

clue.text: Possible feature of a dive's grub

definitions.meaning: the position a diver folds into off the board
school slang for food, the sort sold over a counter at break

explanation.surface: The food you might expect to find in a seedy bar.
explanation.walkthrough: Dive is the seedy bar in the sentence and the header off a board in the definition. British schools have had tuck shops selling sweets and crisps for well over a century.
explanation.definitionFit: In diving, a tuck is the position where the body folds knees to chest, and tuck is also what British schoolchildren call the snacks from the tuck shop.

clue.text: Dubious pressure to oust Democrat, 'Chubby'

indicators.note: To oust somebody is to put them out and stand where they stood, so one letter leaves and the other takes the empty place.

parts.note: something dubious is dodgy, and that whole word is what is being worked on
d is the short form for a Democrat in American reporting, and this is the letter that goes
p is the physicist's short form for pressure, and it moves into the gap

explanation.surface: Political pressure to unseat a Democrat nicknamed Chubby.
explanation.walkthrough: Chubby sits in quotation marks so that it reads as the nickname, and it is the definition. Dubious is not a comment on the pressure: it is the word being operated on.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody podgy is softly overweight, short and round with it, which is what calling them chubby says more kindly.

clue.text: Pull Taylor Swift, say

definitions.meaning: the singer offered as one instance of a nationality

explanation.surface: Trying to get off with Taylor Swift.
explanation.walkthrough: Pull is British slang for getting off with somebody, which is the whole of the surface. Say marks the singer as an example rather than a synonym: she was born in Pennsylvania.
explanation.definitionFit: To yank something is to pull it sharply, and Yank is the standing British nickname for an American, which is what Taylor Swift is.

clue.text: Many accepting Labour Leader should be set aside

indicators.note: To accept something is to let it in, so the words named part and the letter goes between them.

parts.note: a lot of something is many of it, two words run together and parting after the first

indicators.note: A leader stands at the head of what follows, so the letter wanted is the one the word begins with.

parts.note: the letter the party's name begins with, taken as instructed

explanation.surface: Plenty of people agreeing that the Labour leader ought to be shoved aside.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital on Leader makes it Starmer's title and it is the instruction to take a first letter. Set aside is meant in the allotting sense — money or time put by — not the sacking the sentence has in mind.
explanation.definitionFit: To allot is to portion something out and earmark it for a purpose, which is what setting funds or hours aside amounts to.

clue.text: Bill Clinton's no.1 love doctor 'flipped' Unity

indicators.note: Something flipped has been turned over end for end, so the two letters are written in the other order.

parts.note: a bill is an account, written a/c on a bank statement

indicators.note: A person's no.1 is whatever comes first, so the letter wanted is the one the name opens with.

parts.note: the letter the name opens with, taken as instructed
love is the tennis scoreboard's nothing, written as a ring
Dr is the title's short form, turned end for end as instructed

explanation.surface: Bill Clinton's favourite love doctor turning on him.
explanation.walkthrough: Bill Clinton reads as one man and supplies two pieces separately, the bill being an account long before it is a president. Flipped sits in quotation marks because it is doing the turning rather than describing the doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: An accord is a formal agreement that puts the parties on one side, which is unity in the sense of minds brought together.
